prompt: For V = IR, {{1}} the one you want and the formula rearranges itself.
explanation: Cover it. Hiding V leaves I times R; hiding I leaves V over R; hiding R leaves V over I. It is a memory aid for rearranging under pressure, not a physical law.

prompt: A wire is made longer and thinner. What happens to its resistance?

options.text: It rises, because R = ρ L over A means long and thin resists
It falls, because a longer wire carries more current
It is unchanged, because resistivity is a property of the material
It falls, because a smaller area means less material to resist
It rises only if the material is a semiconductor

explanation: R = ρ L/A. Length is on top, so a longer wire resists more; area is underneath, so a thinner wire resists more too. Long and thin resists; short and fat does not. Resistivity ρ is the material property and does not change with shape.

why.a: Correct on both counts, and both changes push the same way here.
why.b: Wrong. Length is in the numerator, so more length means more resistance.
why.c: Wrong. Resistivity is fixed by the material, but RESISTANCE also depends on shape.
why.d: Wrong, and reversed: a smaller cross-section squeezes the current and raises the resistance.
why.e: Wrong. The geometry argument holds for any ohmic material.

prompt: The hook for R = ρ L over A is that long and {{1}} resists, while short and fat does not.
explanation: Thin. Length on top and area underneath, so both being unfavourable raises the resistance.

prompt: You combine three resistors in parallel and get a value LARGER than the smallest of them. What has happened?

options.text: A mistake: parallel resistance is always less than the smallest, so the reciprocal was not flipped back
Nothing: parallel resistance can be larger than the smallest resistor
Nothing, provided the resistors are not equal
The resistors must have been in series instead
The supply voltage was too low

explanation: Adding a parallel path always gives the current somewhere else to go, so the combination must conduct better than any single branch, which means a resistance below the smallest. Getting a larger value almost always means stopping at 1/R without inverting to get R.

why.a: Correct, and this is a free check worth running on every parallel answer.
why.c: Wrong. The rule holds whether or not the resistors are equal.
why.d: Wrong. Series is where resistances add; the question specifies parallel.
why.e: Wrong. The combination does not depend on the supply.

prompt: The equivalent resistance of a parallel combination is always less than the smallest resistor in it.
explanation: True, and it is the fastest sanity check in circuit work. Every extra parallel branch gives the current another route, so the combination always conducts better than the best single branch.

why.true: Correct, and a result above the smallest means the reciprocal was not inverted back.
why.false: Wrong. Parallel paths can only ever lower the total resistance.

prompt: What does each of Kirchhoff’s laws express?

options.text: The current law conserves charge at junctions, and the voltage law conserves energy around loops
The current law conserves energy, and the voltage law conserves charge
Neither is a conservation law; both are experimental rules with no deeper basis

explanation: KCL is charge, KVL is energy. Current in equals current out at a junction because charge cannot pile up there; the voltages around a closed loop sum to zero because a charge returning to its starting point must have gained and lost equal energy.

why.a: Correct. Charge cannot pile up at a junction, and a charge going once round a loop must gain and lose equal energy.
why.c: Wrong. Only the current law is about charge.
why.d: Wrong. Only the voltage law is about energy.
why.e: Wrong. Both follow from conservation principles.

prompt: Kirchhoff’s current law is about charge and his voltage law is about {{1}}.
explanation: Energy. Junctions conserve charge, loops conserve energy: two words that keep the pair straight.
